::: callout-note
## Draft for review — revised August 2026

Prepared for the University of Copenhagen IT department. Alongside it we provide
infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) and operational runbooks so your team can
stand the system up against the resources below, or use them as a costing
reference for your own deployment.

**What changed in this revision.** The first version (June 2026) asked one
question: *can you host this?* Since then, two things have altered the picture.
KU has committed **110 million DKK over three years from 1 September 2026** to
integrating AI across research, teaching and administration, with a new AI
office, a cross-faculty taskforce, AI-labs and a significant strengthening of KU
IT — and KU IT is already building internal infrastructure with locally hosted
models, aiming at a KU-wide AI platform where staff and students sign in with
their KU credentials and choose a model appropriate to the task. Separately,
AIPLA's technical lead is engaged with the project to at least April 2027, so
this document is no longer a farewell handover; it is the opening of a working
conversation.

That changes the question. **Section 4b** is new and is the part we would most
like your response to: it sets out three possible relationships between AIPLA
and the platform KU IT is building — AIPLA as a *tenant* of it, AIPLA as a
*template* for it, or the two built in parallel. We have a view, but it is
yours to decide.
:::

## 1. Purpose

AIPLA (AI in Physics Learning and Assessment) is a three-year research programme
at the Center for Digital Education studying how generative AI can be used in
upper-secondary (stx) physics teaching and assessment. Its software platform has
been running since May 2026, has been in live use with Danish gymnasium teachers
since August 2026, and currently runs on Google Cloud in the EU (Finland region).

This document has two purposes:

1. **To specify what the application needs to run inside University of
   Copenhagen infrastructure** — fully on-premises or hybrid — so your team can
   assess feasibility and estimate effort. Sections 2–3 and 5–6.
2. **To open a decision about the relationship between AIPLA and the KU-wide AI
   platform KU IT is now building.** Section 4b. These are two efforts pointed
   at overlapping problems, and the cheapest outcome for both is almost
   certainly not to build them twice.

It ends with a short set of questions we need answered to firm up either plan.

The application is built on portable, open standards — Linux containers,
PostgreSQL, S3-compatible object storage, OpenID Connect single sign-on, and
open-source model inference. Migrating it is therefore a matter of providing
equivalent infrastructure, **not** rewriting the software.

## 2. What the application is (in brief)

| Component | What it does | Standard technology |
|---|---|---|
| Web application | Student chat interface + teacher dashboard | Linux containers (Next.js + Python) |
| Database | Application data + document-search index | PostgreSQL (with the `pgvector` extension) |
| Object storage | Uploaded documents, optional lesson audio, caches | S3-compatible (e.g. MinIO) or NFS |
| AI model inference | The language models behind the tutor | Open-weight models served on GPUs (or cloud API) |
| Authentication | Teacher sign-in; anonymous student join | Institutional SSO (OIDC/SAML) + anonymous codes |
| Observability | Logs, metrics, traces (kept internal) | OpenTelemetry → Grafana/Prometheus or ELK |

The web application and database are modest in size; the **GPU for model
inference is the main new hardware consideration**, and is covered in sections
5–6.

## 3. Data residency and privacy (why hosting at UCPH is attractive)

This is likely the strongest reason to host internally:

- **No personally identifying student data is collected — by design.** Students
  join a lesson by entering an anonymous group code on a shared device. The
  system stores nothing that identifies an individual student: no names, no
  emails, no device identifiers. The "personal data" category is empty by
  construction, which substantially simplifies data-protection review.
- **Teachers** sign in with institutional credentials (single sign-on).
- **Today** all data is held in the EU (Google Cloud, Finland). **Hosting at
  UCPH** would place all data — including any optional, consent-gated lesson
  recordings — entirely on university infrastructure: the strongest possible
  data-sovereignty posture.

## 4. Hosting options

There is a spectrum between today's full-cloud setup and a fully on-premises
deployment. UCPH does not have to choose the extreme.

| | A. Full cloud (today) | B. Inference on-prem | C. App + data on-prem *(recommended)* | D. Fully on-prem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AI models | Cloud API | UCPH GPUs serve most; cloud for overflow | UCPH GPUs serve most; cloud API only for the hardest tasks | All on UCPH GPUs |
| App + database + storage | Cloud (EU) | Cloud (EU) | **UCPH** | UCPH |
| Student data leaves UCPH? | Stays in EU cloud | Stays in EU cloud | **No** (except a few model prompts) | **No** |
| GPU hardware needed | None | High | Medium (single high-end GPU) | High (GPU cluster) |
| Effort | — | Low–medium | Medium | High |

**Our recommendation is C**: the application and all student data live at UCPH,
while a small set of the most demanding AI tasks may still use an EU cloud model
API until on-premises models are proven equal. **B** is a sensible stepping
stone if GPUs arrive before the rest of the migration. **D** is the end state
once a GPU cluster is in place.

## 4b. Relationship to the KU-wide AI platform

Section 4 asks *where AIPLA's data and models sit*. This section asks a
different question: **what relationship should AIPLA have to the general AI
platform KU IT is building?**

We understand that KU IT is standing up internal infrastructure with locally
hosted models, with the goal of a platform where staff and students sign in with
their KU credentials and select a model suited to the task at hand. AIPLA
already does a version of this for one discipline. There are three ways those
two facts can be resolved, and the choice is KU's.

### Option 1 — AIPLA as a tenant

AIPLA keeps its own application layer and consumes the KU platform for the two
things that are genuinely institutional: **model inference** and **teacher
sign-on**.

- **What KU provides:** an inference endpoint (an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API is
  the common denominator, and is what both vLLM and Ollama serve), and an OIDC
  client registration.
- **What changes in AIPLA:** the model router gains one more provider entry;
  teacher authentication points at the KU identity provider. Both are
  configuration-scale changes rather than rewrites — the router already
  dispatches across three provider families — and the student path needs nothing
  from KU at all, since students are anonymous by design.
- **Effort:** low. Days rather than weeks.
- **What it does not solve:** the two systems still duplicate everything above
  the model call — spend governance, logging, document handling, and the
  per-subject configuration surface.

This is the sensible first step whatever else is decided, and we would like to
do it regardless of the answer to the rest of this section.

### Option 2 — AIPLA as a template for the KU platform

The KU platform takes AIPLA's application layer as its starting point, and AIPLA
becomes the physics instance of it rather than a separate system.

This is worth considering for one specific reason: **AIPLA is already a fork of
a general-purpose platform, not a bespoke physics application.** It was built by
forking a domain-neutral template and adding a physics configuration layer on
top. The separation between "the platform" and "one subject's use of it" is not
a retrospective claim — it is how the code is organised, and the existence of
the fork is evidence that it separates cleanly.

Concretely, the following already exist and are in live use. They are the parts
a general institutional platform needs, rather than the parts specific to
physics:

| Capability | State today |
|---|---|
| **Model routing across providers** | Dispatches across Gemini (Vertex), Claude (Vertex), and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Which model serves which task is a configuration field, not code. |
| **Per-task, per-user spend governance** | A register of who may spend, monthly caps in real currency, tiers, expiry dates, and per-task cost multipliers. Enforced at request time rather than reconciled after the fact. This is usually the hardest part of an institutional AI platform to retrofit. |
| **Two identity modes** | Institutional single sign-on for staff, plus a fully anonymous join path for people who must not be identified. Most platforms have only the first. |
| **Configuration by subject, not by code** | Each use case is a plain-text configuration document — instructions, tools, model tier, budget policy — versioned in a repository and deployed automatically. A department can author one without a developer. |
| **Document handling** | Parsing across 13 deterministic formats plus AI extraction, and retrieval-augmented search over an institutional document corpus with per-corpus access control. |
| **Interactive content** | Sandboxed browser applications (simulations, interactive exercises) inside an enforced security envelope — content-security policy, iframe sandboxing, size limits, no external network access. |
| **Observability and research data** | OpenTelemetry traces, structured logs, and an anonymised interaction log in a queryable analytics store — designed for research use from the start rather than added afterwards. |
| **Open protocols** | Speaks MCP, A2A, AG-UI and A2UI, so it interoperates with tools built elsewhere instead of requiring everything to be built inside it. |
| **Infrastructure as code** | Terraform across three environments with artefact-based promotion, plus a local mode that runs the entire system with no cloud dependency. |

There is also a governance argument, which we raise tentatively because it is
not ours to make. If the intention is that **each subject works out for itself
what AI means for its teaching**, then a platform whose unit of configuration is
*a subject's own plain-text document* is the technical expression of that
policy, where a platform that centralises those decisions is not. AIPLA is a
worked example of one subject doing exactly this, with a live teacher pilot
behind it.

**What we would say against this option, plainly:**

- **Scale is unproven.** AIPLA is sized and tested for roughly ten teachers and
  their classes. Nothing in the architecture forbids institutional scale, but
  nothing in its history demonstrates it either. A KU-wide platform is a
  different engineering problem and we would not want that difference glossed
  over.
- **It carries migration debt.** Three components were chosen for speed of
  delivery and are specific to the current cloud: the application database, the
  retrieval store, and the session store. Our internal migration notes cost this
  honestly. That debt is tolerable in a research prototype and less tolerable in
  a platform other people build on.
- **It is a research prototype, not a supported product.** It has one principal
  developer. Adopting it means either resourcing it as a platform or accepting
  that constraint knowingly.
- **We have an interest.** The same person maintains AIPLA and the template it
  derives from. We are not a neutral party recommending ourselves, and this
  section should be weighed accordingly. The licensing and ownership position of
  the underlying template would need to be settled before anyone built on it.

### Option 3 — parallel systems

KU builds its platform; AIPLA continues as it is. This is a legitimate choice.
It is the lowest-coordination path, and it may simply be that KU IT's
requirements, procurement position, or existing commitments make the other
options moot.

Its cost is duplication in the layers that are institutional rather than
disciplinary: spend governance, logging, document handling, single sign-on, and
the guidance that has to be written for each of them. If this is the direction,
we would like to know early, because it changes what is worth building on the
AIPLA side.

### What we suggest

**Option 1 in the near term, and a conversation about Option 2.** The tenancy
work is small, useful under every scenario, and would give both sides a concrete
integration to learn from before any larger decision is taken. Whether AIPLA is
also a useful starting point for the wider platform is a question we would
rather explore with your team than assert.


## 5. Resource list (what UCPH would provide)

Quantities depend on the hosting option chosen (section 4). Figures are for
pilot scale (roughly 10 teachers and their classes) and are order-of-magnitude
for planning.

**Compute (application — modest):**

- Container hosting: a Kubernetes namespace **or** 1–2 virtual machines running
  Docker. Approximately **4 vCPU / 8 GB RAM total** for the web app, backend,
  and a small document-parsing service.
- A container image registry and a CI runner for builds.

**GPU (AI model inference — the main hardware decision; see section 6):**

- **Option C (recommended):** one high-end GPU (e.g. **NVIDIA H100 80 GB**) for
  the main model — comfortably runs a current single-GPU open-weight model such
  as Qwen 3.6 (27–35B)[^qwen-hw] — plus one smaller GPU (e.g. **L4 / A10, 24 GB**)
  for text-search embeddings and speech-to-text.
- **Option D (full sovereignty):** a cluster of **≈8 × H200** to serve a
  frontier-class open-weight model (e.g. GLM 5.2, ~744B parameters, at FP8 —
  roughly 1.1 TB aggregate VRAM)[^glm-hw], plus the smaller embeddings / speech GPU.
- Inference is served with standard open-source software (vLLM or Ollama).

**Database:**

- **PostgreSQL 15+ with the `pgvector` extension** — serves application data,
  document-search vectors, session state, and analytics. Managed Postgres if
  available; otherwise a standard (ideally highly-available) instance.

**Object storage:**

- **S3-compatible storage (e.g. MinIO) or NFS** — uploaded documents, optional
  lesson recordings, caches. Tens of GB at pilot scale; audio dominates if
  recording is enabled.

**Identity:**

- **Teacher single sign-on** from the UCPH identity provider (OpenID Connect or
  SAML). Students require **no** identity provider (anonymous codes only).

**Supporting services:**

- A secrets store (e.g. HashiCorp Vault or Kubernetes secrets).
- A logging / metrics stack (Grafana + Prometheus / Loki, or ELK).
- Ingress with TLS certificates; a policy decision on whether any external model
  API calls are permitted (relevant only for hybrid options B / C).

## 6. AI models and GPU sizing (the main open decision)

During the pilot the application uses top-tier commercial models for quality.
For self-hosting, these are replaced by **open-weight models** run on UCPH GPUs.
The model choice is being validated by an ongoing capability evaluation against
real physics-tutoring tasks; the **hardware to provision depends on which
hosting option (section 4) UCPH chooses**:

| Tier | Example open-weight model | Hardware | Suitable for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single GPU (Option C floor) | **Qwen 3.6** (27B dense, or 35B-A3B MoE) | 1 × H100 / A100 80 GB (runs at 4-bit on a 24 GB GPU) | Tutor chat, document tasks; the realistic starting point |
| GPU cluster (Option D) | **GLM 5.2** (~744B params / 39B active MoE, 1M context, MIT-licensed — currently the strongest open-weight model) | ≈8 × H200 at FP8 (~1.1 TB aggregate VRAM); BF16 needs more | All tasks including the hardest reasoning; whole-institution scale |
| Supporting GPU | Embeddings + speech-to-text (Whisper) | 1 × 24 GB GPU (or CPU for embeddings) | Document search + voice |

We are happy to walk your team through the evaluation results and recommend a
specific configuration once your GPU availability is known.

### Responsiveness and capacity

Two figures matter, and they answer different questions:

- **Per-student streaming speed** — how fast a single reply appears. Human
  reading is roughly 5–10 tokens per second, so anything above ~20–30 tokens per
  second per student already feels immediate. Both recommended setups exceed
  this comfortably for an individual user.
- **Aggregate throughput** — the total tokens per second served across *all*
  students at once (the serving software batches requests continuously). This is
  the capacity figure.

Recent published benchmarks put a single H100 serving a Qwen-3-class model at
roughly **2,000+ tokens/second aggregate**[^qwen-tput], and an 8 × H200 cluster
serving GLM 5.2 at about **1,200 tokens/second**[^glm-tput] (with speculative
decoding). In practice that means a single H100 comfortably serves a full
classroom concurrently, while each student's reply still streams faster than
they can read.

| Setup | Aggregate throughput | Per-student feel |
|---|---|---|
| Option C — Qwen 3.6 on 1 × H100 | ~2,000+ tokens/s | tens of tokens/s (well above reading speed) |
| Option D — GLM 5.2 on 8 × H200 (FP8) | ~1,200 tokens/s | ~30–60 tokens/s |

**Making responses faster (no extra hardware).** The largest gains for a
tutoring workload come from software, not silicon:

- **Tiered model routing** — most tutoring turns are handled by the smaller,
  faster model (Qwen 3.6), reserving the large model for genuinely hard
  reasoning. The typical reply is then both faster and cheaper.
- **Prefix caching** — the tutor's fixed instructions and lesson context are
  identical every turn, so they are processed once and cached, sharply reducing
  the time to the first word of a reply.
- **Speculative decoding** (e.g. EAGLE) — 1.5–3× faster reply streaming; the
  GLM 5.2 figure above already uses it.
- **FP8 precision** — already assumed in the sizing above.

Newer or additional hardware (e.g. B200) raises both numbers further, but is
only needed if concurrency or large-model latency must improve beyond the above.

## 7. Questions for UCPH IT

The June 2026 version of this document asked whether you could host AIPLA. Since
you are already building internal model infrastructure, the useful questions have
changed. **Group A is the one we would most like answered**; group B remains
relevant if AIPLA is hosted separately from the KU platform.

### A. About the KU platform (new — see section 4b)

1. **Inference access.** Will the KU platform expose model inference to other
   university applications, or only to end users through its own interface? If
   the former, over what interface — an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, or something
   else? What would AIPLA need to do to be admitted as a consumer?
2. **Model catalogue.** Which open-weight models are you planning to serve, at
   what sizes, and on what hardware? We have measured several candidates against
   real Danish stx physics tasks and are happy to share the results, which may be
   useful to you independently of AIPLA (section 8).
3. **Single sign-on.** Which protocol does the UCPH identity provider support for
   application integration — OpenID Connect or SAML? Can AIPLA register as a
   client, and what is the process?
4. **Platform scope.** How far up the stack does the KU platform intend to go?
   Model access and sign-on only, or also spend governance, document corpora,
   logging, and per-department configuration? This determines whether AIPLA is a
   tenant, a template, or a parallel system (section 4b), and it is the single
   answer that most changes what we build next.
5. **Timing.** When do you expect inference and sign-on to be available to other
   applications, even in a limited form? We would rather integrate early against
   something incomplete than late against something finished.

### B. About hosting AIPLA itself

6. **GPU hosting.** Do you have, or can you provision, GPU hosting for model
   inference — a single high-end GPU (Option C) or a cluster (Option D)? What
   specification, and on what timeline? If the KU platform's GPUs serve this
   need, questions 6 and 1 are the same question.
7. **Containers and database.** Do you offer Kubernetes or VM hosting, and a
   managed **PostgreSQL** (ideally with the `pgvector` extension)? Is
   S3-compatible object storage available?
8. **Data-protection precedent.** Is there an existing pattern for
   student-facing services that has already cleared your data-protection review,
   which we could align with rather than starting from scratch?
9. **External connectivity (hybrid only).** For a hybrid setup, is it acceptable
   for the application to call an **EU-hosted** commercial model API for a small
   set of the hardest tasks (sending only the prompt, no student identity), or
   must the deployment be fully self-contained?

## 8. What we can contribute

- This requirements document and the accompanying migration notes.
- **Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform)** plus operational runbooks, so your team
  can stand the system up against the resources above — or read them as a
  costing reference for your own deployment.
- **A capability evaluation of open-weight models on real Danish upper-secondary
  physics tasks**, refreshed as new models release. As of July 2026 it measures
  eleven models on exam problem-solving and nine on figure-reading, in five runs
  each, against published ministry answer keys. Two findings look relevant to
  the KU model catalogue independently of AIPLA: a single-GPU open model already
  clears our usefulness threshold on both text and figures, and **no single open
  model does both well** — a self-hosted tier needs a text model and a
  vision-language model, routed by whether the question carries a figure. This
  is also the evidence base for right-sizing model choice per task, which bears
  directly on both cost and energy use. A standalone summary is available.
- A walkthrough session with your team to answer questions and agree the target
  configuration.

**We are not on a deadline for this.** AIPLA's technical lead is engaged with the
project to at least April 2027, and the system continues to run on EU cloud with
no disruption in the meantime. Integration or migration can proceed at whatever
pace suits your own build. What we would most like in the near term is a
conversation about section 4b, early enough to be useful to both sides.

[^qwen-hw]: Qwen 3.6 sizes and VRAM (27B dense and 35B-A3B MoE; ~17–21 GB at
    4-bit, fits a single 24 GB GPU): *Qwen 3.6 VRAM & Hardware Requirements*,
    Will It Run AI (2026) — <https://willitrunai.com/blog/qwen-3-6-vram-requirements>;
    *Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: Specifications and GPU VRAM*, apxml —
    <https://apxml.com/models/qwen36-35b-a3b>.

[^glm-hw]: GLM 5.2 architecture and VRAM (~744B total / 39B active MoE, 1M-token
    context, MIT-licensed; ~744 GB at FP8, fits one 8 × H200 node): *GLM-5.2
    vLLM recipe* — <https://recipes.vllm.ai/zai-org/GLM-5.2>; *Self-Host GLM 5.2:
    Hardware, vLLM Setup, and Cost*, ofox.ai (2026) —
    <https://ofox.ai/blog/glm-5-2-self-host-vllm-hardware-cost-2026/>; *GLM-5.2
    1M context on a single 8×H200 node*, Phala —
    <https://phala.com/posts/glm-5-2-1m-context-8xh200>.

[^qwen-tput]: Qwen-3-class throughput on a single H100 (~2,352 tokens/s
    aggregate via vLLM): *Optimizing Qwen3-32B Throughput on NVIDIA H100*,
    GPUStack — <https://docs.gpustack.ai/2.0/performance-lab/qwen3-32b/h100/>;
    day-one cost/throughput comparison for Qwen3.6-27B: *Qwen3.6-27B bakeoff*,
    LLMKube — <https://llmkube.com/blog/qwen3-6-27b-bakeoff>.

[^glm-tput]: GLM 5.2 throughput on 8 × H200 (~1,215 tokens/s sustained output,
    FP8, SGLang + EAGLE speculative decoding; ~1,370 tokens/s on 8 × B200):
    *GLM-5-FP8 Inference Benchmark: 8×B200 vs 8×H200* —
    <https://gist.github.com/BenHamm/dcd09f595fef141567a39582f502cef4>.
